title: Ultrasonic Testing for Rail | UT Inspection of Railcars (US)
description: On-site ultrasonic testing of railcar and locomotive axles, castings, welds and tank car thickness across the US. No in-track flaw detection. Request a quote.
h1: Ultrasonic Testing for Rail Equipment and Bridges in the United States
html:
Atlantis NDT performs on-site ultrasonic testing (UT) of railcar and locomotive components in the United States: axles, wheels, bolsters, side frames, couplers, welds and thickness of tank car shells, plus the steel members of railroad bridges. Technicians are mobilized to your car shop, locomotive facility, yard or bridge site. We do not run in-track rail flaw detection. To scope a job, request a UT inspection quote.

What "ultrasonic rail inspection" means, and what we do and do not do

People searching for ultrasonic rail inspection usually mean one of two very different jobs. The first is in-track flaw detection: a detector car or a hi-rail vehicle with transducer wheels or sleds runs over the rail head and web looking for transverse defects, detail fractures and weld flaws. That work is organized around the track safety standards in 49 CFR Part 213, it uses purpose-built test vehicles and trained operators, and it is run by railroads and a small number of specialist service operators. Atlantis does not offer it, and we would rather say so than let you find out on the phone.

The second job is inspection of the equipment that rolls on the track and the structures that carry it. That is conventional contact ultrasonic work done with a portable flaw detector and a handful of probes on parts that are in a shop, on a pad or on a bridge. It is the work on this page. Thickness gauging, straight-beam checks of forged and cast sections, shear-wave scans of welds, and axle examination from the end face all fit a technician who travels to the site with a flaw detector, calibration blocks and a written procedure.

A few related points so the scope is clear from the start. Radiography of welds and castings is not something we perform in the United States, because industrial radiography is licensed under NRC and Agreement State rules; when a drawing calls for it we tell you plainly and suggest ultrasonic examination where the code and your engineer allow it. We also do not set inspection intervals or decide whether equipment returns to service. Your qualified engineer or railroad inspector owns that decision, and our report gives them clean data to make it.

The rules behind the examination

Rail equipment inspection is driven by the Federal Railroad Administration. The main parts are 49 CFR Part 215 for freight car safety standards, Part 229 for locomotives, Part 231 for safety appliances and Part 238 for passenger equipment, with Part 237 covering bridge safety. None of those regulations is an NDT procedure. They set the defects that make a car or locomotive unsafe to operate and the records an owner must keep. The detailed acceptance rules that a shop works to day to day come from the AAR Manual of Standards and Recommended Practices and the interchange rules, which cover wheels, axles, couplers, truck components and the approval of repair facilities.

For the examination itself we work to a written procedure that references the method standards: ASTM E114 for straight-beam contact testing, ASTM E164 for contact testing of weldments, ASTM E797 for thickness measurement and ASME Section V Article 4 for ultrasonic technique requirements where a code invokes it. Where a car builder or repair shop writes its own acceptance table, the table governs and our procedure is written to match it. Our technicians are qualified under Atlantis's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A: a Level II performs and interprets the scan, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report.

Welded repairs and fabrication on cars and locomotives are commonly governed by AWS D15.1, the railroad welding specification, together with the owner's own repair standard. Steel bridge members fall under the owner's bridge management program under Part 237, with engineering design practice following the AREMA manual and welding rules from AWS where they are cited. In each case the acceptance authority is named in the contract documents, not chosen by the inspection company.

Components we examine by ultrasonic testing

Axles. Axle shafts fail by fatigue cracking, usually starting at a press-fit seat, a fillet or a journal. A technician can examine an axle from the end face with a straight beam and angled beams that sweep the journal, the wheel seats and the gear seat on locomotive axles, with the axle held on a stand or still in the wheelset. The calibration reference is a representative axle section or a reference block with machined notches, and the coverage plan is part of the procedure: which probes, from which face, with what scan overlap. Some owners prefer to combine this with magnetic particle inspection of exposed surfaces; the rail magnetic particle page covers that.

Wheels. In a shop, ultrasonic examination of wheel rims looks for subsurface rim defects and for thin or shelled areas that visual inspection cannot size. Rim thickness and flange wear are measured against the limits in the interchange rules. Testing is done on the tread with the wheelset in a stand or on a rolling fixture, because curvature and tread condition must be right for stable coupling.

Cast components. Truck bolsters, side frames and couplers are steel castings, and casting defects such as shrinkage, gas porosity and hot tears sit inside the section. Straight-beam scans through the thick sections of a bolster or a coupler body find volumetric indications that surface methods cannot. Our job page on ultrasonic testing of castings and forgings explains how we handle coarse grain and rough surfaces, which are the main limits on casting examination.

Welds on cars and locomotives. Underframe center sills, draft sill attachments, tank car shell-to-head welds, locomotive frame welds and repair welds on trucks all take shear-wave examination. The weld is mapped, the scan surface is cleaned and marked, and the technician scans the weld and the heat-affected zone from both sides where geometry allows, recording indication location, length and amplitude against the reference level.

Tank car shells and heads. Tank car owners must qualify and maintain tank cars under 49 CFR Part 180 and the AAR tank car standards, and shell thickness is part of that picture. Ultrasonic thickness readings on a grid, with the technician logging each point, give the owner's program a record of metal loss. We provide the readings and the map; the owner's tank car engineer judges them.

Rail bridge members. Steel girders, floor beams, hanger plates and pins are examined where an engineer has called for it, with thickness readings on corroded flanges and webs and shear-wave scans on suspect welds. Access is by the owner's rail-protected arrangement, a bucket truck, scaffold or rope access set by the owner, and a flagman or track protection comes from the railroad.

Technique details that matter in a rail shop

Couplant and surface condition drive repeatability. Painted and scaled steel, cast surfaces and tread surfaces all affect probe coupling, so a technician removes loose scale and flaking paint on the scan path, uses a gel or paste couplant suited to the surface, and records any case where a cast surface limited coupling. Thickness work is done on a flat clean spot, and a technician either measures through intact coating after verifying on a coated reference or removes the coating at the reading point, as the procedure states.

Calibration is checked at the start of each shift and any time a probe, cable or instrument is changed, using a step wedge for thickness and a reference block or reference axle for flaw detection. Axle and bolster scans need a reference level the owner agrees to before the job starts, because "a reject" depends on the reference. Casting scans need a back-wall reflection check to prove the sound path, and loss of back wall is recorded as a coupling or attenuation problem and not read as a pass.

Temperature matters on locomotive exhaust components and freshly welded repairs. We keep the part within the range the couplant and probe allow, and where the part is hot a high-temperature couplant is used with calibration done at working temperature.

How UT compares with magnetic particle and penetrant testing here

Choosing a method for common railcar and locomotive components
ComponentUltrasonic testingMagnetic particlePenetrant
Axle journals and seatsFinds cracks growing under press-fit seatsFinds surface cracks on exposed steelNot used on steel axles in most shops
Couplers and knucklesFinds internal casting flaws in thick sectionsFinds surface-breaking cracks and lapsAlternative on non-magnetic or coated parts
Bolsters and side framesThickness and internal flawsPrimary method for surface cracks at cornersUsed on aluminum and stainless parts
Tank car shellsPrimary method for wall thicknessWeld toes and attachmentsLimited use
Bridge membersThickness, pins, weld interiorWeld toes and fatigue detailsNot typical

The sibling pages cover those columns in depth: magnetic particle inspection for rail and penetrant testing for rail. A short scope that combines two methods on the same component is often simpler to mobilize than two separate visits, so tell us which components you have and we will propose the combination that matches your acceptance table.

What the report contains

Every ultrasonic report we issue carries the same set of facts so that a railroad inspector, a shop quality manager or an outside auditor can retrace the examination.

  • Component identification: car or locomotive number, part number, casting or serial number, and location on the unit.
  • The written procedure number and revision, with the code or acceptance table it follows.
  • The instrument, probes, cables and couplant, with serial numbers and the date of the last calibration or verification.
  • The reference block, step wedge or reference axle used, and the reference level set.
  • The technician's name and level under the written practice, and the Level III who approved the procedure.
  • Scan plan or sketch showing coverage, plus any area that could not be scanned and why.
  • Each indication with location, length, depth where measured and amplitude against the reference, and the accept or reject call against the named criteria.
  • Thickness grids where applicable, with minimum readings highlighted against the nominal and minimum allowable values supplied by the owner.

Reports are reviewed by an ASNT Level III before release, and photographs of marked components are attached when the owner asks for them.

What to send for a quote

A good quote request saves a call. Send these items and we can propose a scope quickly.

  1. Component list or drawing numbers, with quantity and material (cast steel, forged steel, aluminum).
  2. The code, interchange rule or owner standard the work is examined to, and any acceptance table.
  3. Whether parts are loose in a shop, installed on cars or locomotives, or on a bridge structure.
  4. Surface condition, coating thickness if known, and temperature.
  5. Site address, badging, railroad contractor safety orientation and track protection needs.
  6. The dates your outage, shop slot or bridge work window allows.

Planning for a rail site

Rail facilities run on their own safety rules. Contractor orientation, roadway worker protection training where work is near live track, hearing and eye protection around hammer and press operations, and restricted access to car storage tracks are usual. Locomotive shops add fuel, oil and traction power hazards. Bridge work brings fall protection, rail traffic protection and, over water, boat or rigging access. We confirm those requirements before the technicians mobilize and we do not assume that a prior orientation at another site carries over.

Shop work is easiest to plan around the car or locomotive cycle: parts come off, are cleaned and then inspected, and an examination slot is easier to hold when the cleaning is part of the sequence. Weather matters for bridge work and for yards: wet scan surfaces and wind-blown dust affect couplant and instrument handling, so an outdoor examination plan includes a fallback day set by your schedule and not by ours.

Where we work in the United States for rail

Technicians travel to the site for rail equipment work across the country. Cities where we most often scope it:

  • Chicago: the nation's busiest rail interchange, with large classification yards and heavy car repair activity.
  • Kansas City: a central gateway with several major railroads and a large intermodal and car-handling base.
  • Omaha: a long-standing railroad corridor city with major yards and repair facilities.
  • Fort Worth: big yards, locomotive servicing and car repair in North Texas.
  • Jacksonville: Southeast rail connected to port traffic and a heavy equipment presence.
  • Atlanta: a Southern hub for classification and intermodal operations.
  • Norfolk: coal and intermodal rail at the Hampton Roads port complex.
  • St. Louis: river crossings, large bridges and extensive interchange.
  • Memphis: multiple railroads meeting at the Mississippi River with a big intermodal presence.

Our general guidance for choosing a method is in the ultrasonic testing guide, and the national ultrasonic testing page covers the method across industries.

Training your own technicians

Many rail shops would rather qualify their own inspectors and call us for surge work, audits or procedure writing. We offer SNT-TC-1A-based UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training, a practice environment in the ultrasonic testing simulator, and procedure and written practice support through written practice development. Under SNT-TC-1A your employer certifies its personnel, so the written practice is yours; we help build it so it stands up in an audit.

faq.q: Do you perform ultrasonic rail inspection of track?
faq.a: No. In-track rail flaw detection, done with detector cars and hi-rail vehicles under the track safety standards in 49 CFR Part 213, is specialist work we do not offer. We inspect railcar and locomotive components, tank car shells and steel bridge members.

faq.q: Can you examine axles for cracks without pressing the wheels off?
faq.a: Often yes. A technician can scan from the axle end face with straight and angled beams to cover journals and seats, depending on the axle design, the access, and the reference level your standard sets. The procedure states what can and cannot be covered.

faq.q: Which standard decides whether a casting or weld indication is rejected?
faq.a: The acceptance criteria named in your contract or repair standard decide it, not us. That is usually an owner specification, an AAR requirement or a welding code such as AWS D15.1 for railroad welding. Our report records the indication and compares it to that table.

faq.q: What can UT measure on a tank car?
faq.a: Ultrasonic thickness readings on a grid across shells and heads, with a minimum reading recorded against the nominal and minimum allowable values the owner supplies. The owner's tank car program under 49 CFR Part 180 and the AAR tank car standards decides what the numbers mean.

faq.q: Why can't UT find every defect in a bolster or coupler?
faq.a: Cast steel has coarse grain and rough surfaces that scatter sound, so small flaws can be hidden and back-wall loss may occur. We record any area where coupling or attenuation limited the scan, and surface-breaking cracks are better covered by magnetic particle inspection.

We examine steel members where the owner's engineer has called for it: thickness on corroded flanges and webs, pins, and weld interiors. Rail traffic protection and access come from the owner and railroad. Bridge safety is governed by 49 CFR Part 237, and the engineer owns the condition rating.

faq.q: Can your technicians work inside a railroad yard or locomotive shop?
faq.a: Yes, after the contractor orientation, badging and any roadway worker protection training the facility requires. We confirm those requirements before mobilizing, and work near live track follows the railroad's protection rules, not ours.

faq.q: Can you perform radiography on rail castings or welds?
faq.a: Not in the United States. Industrial radiography here is licensed under NRC and Agreement State rules, and Atlantis does not perform it. Where the code and your engineer allow ultrasonic examination as the volumetric method, we propose it instead.

faq.q: What do you need from us to quote a rail UT job?
faq.a: A component list with drawing or part numbers, the material, the governing code or owner standard with its acceptance table, access and condition of the parts, site address and any site safety orientation, and the dates your shop or outage allows.
